questions.q: According to this lesson, when is a Chapter-2-style custom tool (defined directly in your own application) the right choice over building an MCP server?
options: Never — MCP should always be used instead
Only when the tool has no parameters
When the tool is specific to one application, needs the tightest possible latency, or you're still prototyping
Only when working in a language other than Python
questions.explain: A one-off, application-specific tool, or a tool you're still prototyping, doesn't benefit from the overhead of standing up a separate server — the direct Chapter 2 approach is appropriate.

questions.q: Before building a new MCP server, what should you check first, per this lesson?
options: Whether a maintained MCP server for this purpose already exists, like the Filesystem Server or Sentry's official server
Nothing — always build from scratch
Whether your team has a logo for the new server
Whether the feature has ever been requested by a user
questions.explain: MCP's ecosystem already includes real reference and officially maintained servers. Connecting to one that already exists is almost always less work and risk than reimplementing it.

questions.q: Why does "more than one AI application might want this integration" favor building an MCP server over a custom tool?
options: It doesn't — the number of potential users is irrelevant to this decision
MCP servers are always faster than custom tools regardless of use case
Custom tools cannot technically support more than one user
Building it once as an MCP server avoids the M x N integration problem by letting many applications share the same server
questions.explain: This connects directly back to the M x N problem from the first lesson of this chapter: a shared integration built once as a server avoids rebuilding the same thing per application.

questions.q: What does Chapter 4 (Agent Architectures & Patterns) assume about where an agent's tools come from?
options: That all tools must come from an MCP server from that point forward
Nothing specific — architecture patterns like ReAct, planning, and multi-agent systems apply the same way regardless of whether tools are custom-defined or sourced from a connected MCP server
That Chapter 2's tool-calling skills are no longer relevant after this chapter
That only resources, never tools, can be used going forward
questions.explain: The architecture patterns in the next chapter operate on whatever tools an agent has access to — they don't care whether those tools were hand-defined or discovered from an MCP server.

questions.q: A startup is building a one-off internal script that only their own small application will ever call. Per this lesson's framework, what's the better default?
options: Build a full MCP server regardless of the overhead
Neither approach works for this situation
A direct, Chapter-2-style custom tool, since there's no second application that would benefit from sharing it
Always ask a user to approve the architecture choice before writing any code
questions.explain: With no sign this integration will ever be useful outside the one application, and nothing suggesting it should become shared infrastructure, the direct custom-tool approach is the better default per the lesson's decision questions.
